chunks.text: 2.2 Single-Cell Modeling and Synthesis A complementary line of work models individual cells, but each leaves a controllability gap that our framework targets. Early GAN-based methods such as CytoGAN [ Goldsborough et al.(2017)Goldsborough, Pawlowski, Caicedo, Singh, and Carpenter ] generate single-cell images without any conditioning, and so offer no control over how the generated cell looks. CP2Image [ Ji et al.(2024)Ji, Cutiongco, Jensen, and Yuan ] takes a different approach: the user provides a long vector of standard measurements of cell appearance (the CellProfiler [ Stirling et al.(2021)Stirling, Swain-Bowden, Lucas, Carpenter, Cimini, and Goodman ] representation, on the order of several hundred numbers), and the model generates a matching cell image. In principle this allows the user to specify a target appearance, but in practice the measurements are highly correlated, and [ Ji et al.(2024)Ji, Cutiongco, Jensen, and Yuan ] reports that fewer than a third of them are faithfully reflected in the generated image. As a result, the user cannot reliably make the generated cell, for example, larger or brighter on demand. Cascaded diffusion for cell synthesis [ Yilmaz et al.(2025)Yilmaz, Keven, Wu, and Stegmaier ] takes yet another route: it samples a binary cell-shape mask and then fills it in with a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion model. The mask sampler is unconditional, so the user cannot specify the shape, and once a mask is given everything else (brightness, texture, internal structure) is left to the diffusion model; the pipeline is designed for generating training data for cell segmentation rather than for controlling phenotype. Unsupervised single-cell representation learning [ Lafarge et al.(2019)Lafarge, Caicedo, Carpenter, Pluim, Singh, and Veta ] learns compact representations of cell images, but does not generate.

In all of these methods, the input the user can manipulate and the model’s internal representation are designed independently, with no shared set of interpretable directions tied to how cells look. We design both together so that a small set of intuitive controls (size, elongation, brightness, texture) drives both ends, making per-cell phenotype controllable in a stable and interpretable way. 3.3 Biological Conditioning for Latent Diffusion Models We now plug the BioVAE encoder into a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) [ Rombach et al.(2022)Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, and Ommer ] to generate new single-cell images. The pre-trained BioVAE acts as a fixed encoder, projecting each image into a compact latent z z . A denoising network ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} then learns to iteratively remove Gaussian noise ϵ \epsilon from the latent, and we condition the denoising network on the biological signal that the user provides. We compare two choices of conditioning signal: the full 61-dimensional measurement vector v v , and the 15 aggregated semantic axes s s . The first uses every measurement directly; the second uses only the aggregated, intuitive controls. The denoising network is trained with the standard conditional latent diffusion objective: ℒ LDM = 𝔼 z , t , ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) ​ [ ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ​ ( z t , t , s ) ‖ 2 2 ] \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LDM}}=\mathbb{E}_{z,t,\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left[||\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{t},t,s)||_{2}^{2}\right] , where z t z_{t} is the noisy latent at timestep t t , and s s (or alternatively v v ) is the conditioning signal. Because the BioVAE latent and the semantic axes are both aligned with the same set of measurements, moving along any axis at conditioning time produces a consistent and interpretable change in the generated cell.

4 Experiments We evaluated our proposed single-cell generation pipeline on the LIVECell dataset [ Edlund et al.(2021)Edlund, Jackson, Khalid, Bevan, Dale, Dengel, Ahmed, Trygg, and Sjögren ] through three main experiments. First, we ablate the loss components of BioVAE to assess their impact on image reconstruction quality and on how well the latent space is organized along biological measurements. Second, we evaluate the generative quality of the single-cell LDM, comparing conditioning on the raw 61-dimensional measurements against conditioning on the 15 semantic axes, and complement this with a blind study in which biologists assess the realism of generated cells. Finally, we evaluate per-axis controllability through traversal experiments, in which we vary a single semantic axis at a time and measure whether the generated cells change in the expected direction. 4.1 Experimental Setup Dataset: We isolated individual cells using their respective annotation masks, setting backgrounds to black and removing edge fragments. At the instance level, the LIVECell dataset yields 64 × 64 64\times 64 grayscale crops partitioned into 928k training, 166k validation, and 411k test images. Evaluation Metrics: To evaluate reconstruction fidelity , we used MSE, PSNR, SSIM, and rFID. MSE and PSNR assessed pixel-level accuracy, SSIM evaluated structural consistency, and rFID (reconstruction FID [ Heusel et al.(2017)Heusel, Ramsauer, Unterthiner, Nessler, and Hochreiter ] ) captured perceptual realism using deep features. To assess latent space quality , we measured k k -NN neighborhood preservation and linear SVM classification accuracy for cell types.

For the generative performance of our diffusion model, we implemented domain-specialized FID [ Heusel et al.(2017)Heusel, Ramsauer, Unterthiner, Nessler, and Hochreiter ] , MMD [ Gretton et al.(2012)Gretton, Borgwardt, Rasch, Schölkopf, and Smola ] , Precision, and Recall [ Sajjadi et al.(2018)Sajjadi, Bachem, Lucic, Bousquet, and Gelly ] for a quantitative measurement. BioVAE: Our foundational encoder was based on the Stable Diffusion VAE [ Rombach et al.(2022)Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, and Ommer , van den Oord et al.(2017)van den Oord, Vinyals, and Kavukcuoglu , Razavi et al.(2019)Razavi, van den Oord, and Vinyals ] architecture with a downscale factor of 8 and a latent shape of 8 × 8 × 4 8\times 8\times 4 . Training used the Adam optimizer with learning rate of 1.0 × 10 − 4 1.0\times 10^{-4} for 500k iterations with a batch size of 64. Standard loss weights were set to λ Recon = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{Recon}}=1 , λ KL = 10 − 6 \lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}=10^{-6} , and λ GAN = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{GAN}}=1 . BioVAE additionally applied λ Bio = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{Bio}}=1 and λ Entropy = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{Entropy}}=1 . Single-Cell Diffusion: We trained a conditional LDM for 500K iterations using a batch size of 64 and the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} . Biological conditioning (measurements v v or semantic axes s s ) was integrated via FiLM [ Perez et al.(2018)Perez, Strub, de Vries, Dumoulin, and Courville ] . At training, we used 1000 steps for the linear noise scheduler, and we synthesized synthetic single-cells using a DDPM [ Ho et al.(2020)Ho, Jain, and Abbeel ] sampler. 4.2 Implementation Details Boundary handling. Cells were cropped using their segmentation masks with the background set to zero, then padded to 64 × 64 64\times 64 . To prevent the model from latching onto sharp mask boundaries as a shortcut, we applied a 2-pixel Gaussian feathering along the mask edge during training.

We did not observe artifacts at the boundary in generated samples (Fig. 3 ). Domain-specialized image quality evaluation. We used a DINOv2 ViT-S/14 backbone fine-tuned on LIVECell single-cell crops for 50 epochs with a self-supervised iBOT objective, following the default setup adapted to low-resolution images [ Oquab et al.(2023)Oquab, Darcet, Moutakanni, Vo, Szafraniec, Khalidov, Fernandez, Haziza, Massa, El-Nouby, et al. ] . MSE relative to the variant without it (6.82 vs 6.62), reflecting the designed competition between the descriptor-regression force, which pulls biologically similar latents together, and the dispersion force, which spreads them apart. In exchange, the full BioVAE achieves a better balance between reconstruction accuracy and latent structure, providing a more suitable representation for controllable generation. We further analyze the latent topology using k-NN neighborhood preservation and linear SVM classification accuracy. Although absolute values remain small due to the large evaluation set ( > > 160k cells), relative gains indicate improved phenotype-aware organization. Linear classification accuracy also increases by ∼ \sim 1% ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). Entropy regularization contributes to this effect by discouraging collapsed embeddings, while the Bio loss promotes a more structured latent geometry, supporting its use as the encoder backbone for conditional diffusion.

Semantic axes consistently outperform morphodynamic descriptors, approximately halving FID (0.93–0.97 vs 2.04–2.12), with BioVAE + semantic axes achieving the best performance (FID 0.93, MSE 0.925). Interestingly, while BioVAE underperforms the baseline VAE when conditioned on the highly correlated 61-dimensional vector, it demonstrates superior fidelity when paired with the 15-dimensional semantic axes. This suggests that because BioVAE’s latent space already strongly encodes phenotypic structure, conditioning directly on the redundant 61-dimensional vector causes information interference.

The compact, biologically meaningful 15-dimensional semantic axes alleviate this redundancy, creating a favorable synergy with the biologically regularized latent space. Fig. 3 (a) shows representative generated cells, and Fig. 3 (b) highlights challenging cases with partial organelle detail loss. Notably, the “VAE + morphodynamic (61-d)” configuration in Table 3 instantiates the core design choices of prior descriptor-to-image methods — an unstructured latent space conditioned on a high-dimensional, correlated feature vector [ Ji et al.(2024)Ji, Cutiongco, Jensen, and Yuan ] . Our full model (BioVAE + semantic axes) differs precisely along the two axes we ablate: latent regularization and conditioning structure. The 2 × \times 2 ablations therefore double as a controlled comparison against that design paradigm, under a single shared encoder, evaluator, and protocol. 4.5 Blind Study with Biologists A blind study with six biologists evaluated 960 cell instances across eight cell types. Participants classified each cell as real or synthetic, predicted its cell type, and rated task difficulty on a 0–4 scale. Overall discrimination accuracy was 50.9% (AUC = 0.509), which was not significantly different from random guessing (binomial p = 0.58 p=0.58 ). As shown in Fig. 4 (a), synthetic samples were frequently perceived as real: only 20.2% of synthetic cells were correctly identified as synthetic, whereas 81.7% of real cells were correctly classified as real. To quantify perceived realism at the sample level, we defined a realism score as the fraction of observers classifying a cell as real. Real and synthetic cells exhibited comparable realism score distributions, with no significant difference between groups (Mann–Whitney p = 0.41 p=0.41 ; Fig. 4 (b)). Observers generally rated the task as difficult (mean difficulty of 3.17/4), and their ratings were not significantly correlated with discrimination accuracy ( r = 0.14 r=0.14 , p = 0.34 p=0.34 ).

Together, these results indicate that generated single-cell images are visually realistic and preserve morphology consistent with the target phenotypes. Combined with the quantitative analyses above, the study supports the ability of semantic-axis conditioning on BioVAE latents to produce high-quality, phenotype-aligned single-cell images while maintaining biological interpretability. (b) Distribution of realism scores for real and synthetic images. 4.6 Controllability via Axis Traversal Beyond image quality, we explored the controllability properties of the BioVAE + semantic axes latent diffusion model. Unlike the biological feature representation, the semantic axes provide a compact and interpretable phenotype space that enables controllability analysis through biologically meaningful semantic traversals. For this experiment, we sampled 100 representative validation cells, referred to as anchors, and generated semantic traversals by modifying one semantic axis at a time while keeping the remaining axes fixed. The semantic axes were designed to prioritize biological interpretability rather than orthogonal latent decomposition; therefore, the controllability analysis should be interpreted as biologically consistent semantic modulation within a correlated phenotype manifold rather than fully disentangled control. To quantitatively evaluate semantic controllability, we measured three complementary properties: target controllability, control gain, and selectivity. Target controllability was estimated using the Spearman correlation between requested and measured semantic values. Control gain was estimated using the slope of a linear regression between requested and generated semantic values. Finally, selectivity measures the relative dominance of the target semantic response compared to the average response of the non-target semantic axes. Fig.

5 presents representative semantic traversals from a shared anchor cell. The quantitative results are summarized in the Supplementary Sec. C, with additional anchor examples. Figure 5: Representative semantic traversals generated from three validation anchor cells. Each line plot shows the measured semantic-axis response across the traversal range, with their corresponding generated cell images. Dashed red lines indicate the semantic value of the original anchor cell. The traversal results reveal multiple controllability regimes across the semantic space. Cell size, global shape complexity, and symmetry exhibited high target controllability, strong control gain, and moderate selectivity, suggesting that the model can effectively manipulate global morphological structure. Elongation, boundary irregularity, and intensity contrast also presented high target controllability but lower control gain, indicating compressed semantic responses relative to the requested traversal range. We attribute this behavior to the model remaining close to the learned biological manifold and preserving biologically plausible phenotype combinations during generation, consistent with the high precision and recall observed in Section 4.4 . In contrast, shape compactness and granularity exhibited weak target controllability, low control gain, and low selectivity, suggesting limited semantic responsiveness. Interestingly, axes such as edge strength, texture heterogeneity, and intensity skewness presented low target controllability but comparatively high selectivity. This behavior suggests that the model can induce localized semantic perturbations for these descriptors, although without consistently following the requested traversal direction. These axes are strongly correlated with other semantic descriptors and partially reuse related biological features, making isolated manipulation intrinsically more difficult.

Whole-image and single-cell generation address complementary aspects of microscopy. Whole-image models capture spatial organization and cell-to-cell context, whereas single-cell models provide direct control over the appearance of individual cells.

Our framework focuses on the latter and therefore does not model interactions between neighboring cells or larger tissue context. In addition, our evaluation is restricted to LIVECell, which contains phase-contrast images from eight cell lines. Extending the framework to fluorescence, brightfield, 3D imaging, and multi-cellular scenes is an important direction for future work. Why the input and latent representation should be designed together. A central finding is that biologically structuring the latent representation alone is insufficient. BioVAE does not improve generation when paired with the full 61-dimensional measurement vector; its benefit emerges when conditioning is also organized through the 15 semantic axes (Sec. 4.4). This suggests that controllability is a property of the overall pipeline rather than of a single component. More broadly, our results indicate that simple biological priors can improve not only interpretability but also representation structure and conditional generation quality (Tables 2–3). Scope of the semantic axes. The semantic axes provide a compact set of named, measurable, and traversable controls over cell appearance, but they are not a complete description of cellular phenotype. Fine-grained organelle structure, sub-cellular spatial patterns, and biological state transitions are not explicitly represented. Moreover, the axes are manually constructed from standard measurements, so their coverage depends on what those measurements capture. Data-driven extensions using richer assays such as Cell Painting may provide additional biologically meaningful control directions. External comparison. Our evaluation relies primarily on controlled internal ablations rather than direct comparison with external single-cell generators, because existing methods do not provide compatible single-cell-level metrics, feature extractors, or generation protocols on LIVECell.

Establishing a common benchmark for controllable single-cell generation therefore remains an important community-level direction. 6 Conclusion We presented a framework for microscopy generation that operates at the level of individual cells and designs the user-facing controls and the model’s internal representation together, so that both are organized along the same set of biologically meaningful directions. On the input side, we aggregate standard cell measurements into a small set of semantic axes that are each named, measurable, and traversable. On the model side, BioVAE aligns its latent space with the same measurements. On LIVECell, this co-design substantially improves generation quality over conditioning on raw high-dimensional measurements, produces single cells that biologists cannot reliably distinguish from real ones in a blind study, and supports stable per-axis control verified through traversal experiments. We see controllable single-cell generation as a complementary building block alongside whole-image approaches, one that connects classical quantitative cell biology to modern generative modeling and opens a research direction toward biologically grounded, controllable microscopy synthesis.
